ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50656")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50656")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GodDamn Ransomware Uses PoisonX Driver to Disable Endpoint Defenses

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 16 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a new ransomware family called GodDamn that employs the PoisonX kernel driver to neutralize security software as part of its defense evasion strategy. According to a new report published by the Threat Hunter Team from Symantec, the ransomware was first publicly spotted in the wild on May 21, 2026. It's assessed to be a rebrand of the Beast ransomware,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GodDamn Ransomware Uses PoisonX Driver to Disable Endpoint Defenses
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PoisonX BYOVD kernel driver (g11.sys) load / drop by GodDamn ransomware · [LLM] Masquerading 'symantec.exe' user-mode EDR-killer (fake Symantec company info) · [LLM] AnyDesk deployed as silent auto-start service (GodDamn reusable installer) · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NirSoft-based credential harvesting toolkit execution (browsers, VNC, Wi-Fi, mail, sniffer) · [LLM] GodDamn ransomware mass file rename to .God8Damn extension · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
PoisonX BYOVD kernel driver (g11.sys) load / drop by GodDamn ransomware AIInstallation High
Hunts the load or drop of the Microsoft-signed malicious PoisonX kernel driver 'g11.sys' that GodDamn (Hyadina/Beast rebrand) uses in a bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver attack to blind EDR from kernel space. Pivots on the exact driver filename plus the article's file hash rather than a generic BYOVD template. Rationale: g11.sys is the exact PoisonX driver filename named in the article and confirmed across Symantec/GentleKiller reporting; combined with the pre-extracted SHA256 this is a named-binary indicator with near-zero legitimate occurrence. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/the-gentlemen-raas-uses-gentlekiller.html • https://securityaffairs.com/193941/malware/inside-gentlekiller-the-edr-killer-powering-the-gentlemen.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1211 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party driver coincidentally named g11.sys (rare — verify Microsoft signature + WHQL status and cross-check the SHA256)
  • Security-vendor sandbox/detonation host loading the sample for analysis
  • Purple-team BYOVD exercise dropping the same driver
  • Threat-intel/malware-research workstation with the sample on disk
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loaded module is g11.sys and pull SHA256; if it matches a90c3433... treat as confirmed BYOVD. Identify InitiatingProcess and account. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the driver hash via ASR/WDAC, and add g11.sys to the Microsoft Vulnerable Driver Blocklist; kernel-level EDR blinding means the host is likely already partially uninstrumented. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for g11.sys and symantec.exe, for AnyDesk service installs, and for NirSoft credential-harvester execution on the same and adjacent hosts (this actor stages ransomware after EDR is neutralized).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "g11.sys"
    or SHA256 == "a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4697, 7045)
| where ServiceFileName has "g11.sys"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 5f2a9c14-6d3b-4e77-9a1c-2b8f0c7e4d10
description: Detects load or presence of the Microsoft-signed malicious PoisonX driver g11.sys used by GodDamn/Hyadina ransomware to disable EDR from kernel space.

Masquerading 'symantec.exe' user-mode EDR-killer (fake Symantec company info) AIInstallation High
Hunts the GodDamn user-mode defense-evasion tool that impersonates a Symantec product by naming itself symantec.exe while carrying no genuine Symantec/Broadcom version metadata. Excludes real Symantec/Broadcom-signed binaries to isolate the impostor killer. Rationale: The article explicitly states the killer is 'dressed as a Symantec product (symantec.exe)'; a process named symantec.exe with non-Symantec/Broadcom company metadata (or run from a non-standard path) is a high-fidelity masquerade indicator with minimal legitimate footprint. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver.html • https://thomasharris6.wordpress.com/2026/07/09/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver-to-disable-endpoint-defenses/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Symantec/Broadcom Endpoint Protection helper running from a non-standard install path
  • SCCM/Intune packaging that renames a legit Symantec installer to symantec.exe (check signature)
  • Internal IT wrapper script named symantec.exe for AV troubleshooting
  • Security-tool inventory scanner labelled symantec.exe
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Symantec","Broadcom")) and FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the file's digital signature and CompanyName; a valid Broadcom/Symantec Authenticode signature clears it, an unsigned or mismatched binary confirms the killer. Check FolderPath (Temp/ProgramData/Public = suspicious). 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the SHA256, and verify EDR agent processes are still running and reporting. 3) Hunt: on confirmation, look on the same host for g11.sys (PoisonX), AnyDesk service install, and NirSoft harvester execution — symantec.exe typically runs immediately before the encryptor.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "symantec.exe"
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Symantec", "Broadcom"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine,
          ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\symantec.exe"
| where NewProcessName !contains "\\Program Files\\Symantec"
     and NewProcessName !contains "\\Program Files\\Broadcom"
     and NewProcessName !contains "\\Program Files (x86)\\Symantec"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Masquerading symantec.exe EDR-Killer (GodDamn Ransomware)

NirSoft-based credential harvesting toolkit execution (browsers, VNC, Wi-Fi, mail, sniffer) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the NirSoft-derived credential harvester GodDamn operators run before deploying ransomware, which pulls secrets from browsers, Windows Credential Manager, VNC, email clients, Wi-Fi profiles and live network traffic. Pivots on the specific NirSoft tool filenames and the 'NirSoft' version-info company string. Rationale: The article's description of the harvester (browsers + Credential Manager + cached domain creds + VNC + email + Wi-Fi + live traffic) maps precisely onto the NirSoft tool family; matching those specific binary names and the 'NirSoft' CompanyName isolates the toolkit while smartsniff.exe covers the 'live network traffic' capability. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver.html • https://thomasharris6.wordpress.com/2026/07/09/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver-to-disable-endpoint-defenses/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1555 T1040 T1003.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin legitimately recovering a forgotten Wi-Fi/VNC/browser password with a NirSoft utility
  • Help-desk credential-recovery workflow
  • Penetration test using NirSoft tooling
  • Forensics/DFIR analyst running these tools on an evidence host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","anydesk.exe") or IsInitiatingProcessRemoteSession == true
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user context — an interactive admin recovering one password differs from a burst of multiple NirSoft tools launched by a scripted/remote parent (powershell/cmd/psexec). Check parent process and whether output files (e.g. .txt/.csv dumps) were written. 2) Contain: isolate the host and force-reset every credential class the tools can reach (domain, browser-saved, VNC, Wi-Fi PSKs) for affected accounts. 3) Hunt: pivot to co-located symantec.exe / g11.sys / AnyDesk deployment on the host and to any PsExec-driven spread to adjacent hosts; harvested creds fuel this actor's lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName =~ "NirSoft"
    or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "NirSoft"
    or FileName in~ ("webbrowserpassview.exe","mailpv.exe","vncpassview.exe","wirelesskeyview.exe","netpass.exe","iepv.exe","chromepass.exe","passwordfox.exe","netresview.exe","credentialsfileview.exe","smartsniff.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("webbrowserpassview.exe","mailpv.exe","vncpassview.exe","wirelesskeyview.exe","netpass.exe","iepv.exe","chromepass.exe","passwordfox.exe","netresview.exe","credentialsfileview.exe","smartsniff.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AnyDesk deployed as silent auto-start service (GodDamn reusable installer) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts GodDamn's persistence/remote-access step: AnyDesk installed unattended with auto-start-on-boot and a preset password, frequently launched by a pre-staged PowerShell installer and registered as a Windows service to survive reboots. Pivots on AnyDesk's specific unattended install flags rather than mere AnyDesk presence. Rationale: The article states AnyDesk was set up on each host and 'registered as an auto-start Windows service' via a pre-staged PowerShell installer; AnyDesk invoked with --install/--start-with-win/--silent/--set-password is the concrete unattended-deployment signature that separates attacker staging from an interactive user launch. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver.html • https://thomasharris6.wordpress.com/2026/07/09/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver-to-disable-endpoint-defenses/
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.003 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP/IT department deploying AnyDesk fleet-wide via its own silent installer and GPO
  • Sanctioned unattended AnyDesk rollout with --start-with-win for remote support
  • Software packaging system (SCCM/Intune) installing AnyDesk
  • AnyDesk auto-update re-registering the service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has "--set-password"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm AnyDesk is not a sanctioned remote-support tool in this environment; check the parent process (a powershell.exe/cmd.exe pre-staged installer parent is a strong attacker signal) and whether --set-password was used to plant an attacker-controlled unattended password. 2) Contain: stop and disable the AnyDesk service, block the AnyDesk client, and pull AnyDesk connection logs (ad.trace / connection_trace.txt) to identify the attacker relay ID/IP. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts with the same silent-install signature (article reports ~10 hosts in one org) and correlate with PsExec activity, symantec.exe, g11.sys and reboot sequences that follow each install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "anydesk.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--install", "--start-with-win", "--silent", "--set-password")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\anydesk.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--install", "--start-with-win", "--silent", "--set-password")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GodDamn ransomware mass file rename to .God8Damn extension AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the encryption/impact stage where GodDamn renames victim files with the .God8Damn extension at scale. Uses a per-host mass-rename threshold on the article-specific extension to turn the impact event into an alertable signal. Rationale: .God8Damn is the article's named encryption extension for Hyadina/GodDamn attacks; a single host renaming 20+ files to that extension is an unambiguous encryption-in-progress indicator with essentially no legitimate cause. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver.html • https://thomasharris6.wordpress.com/2026/07/09/goddamn-ransomware-uses-poisonx-driver-to-disable-endpoint-defenses/
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate application or user coincidentally saving files with a .God8Damn suffix (implausible at 20+ files)
  • Backup/restore of already-encrypted files from a prior incident replaying the extension
  • Malware-analysis host detonating the sample
  • IR team restaging encrypted samples for triage
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the InitiatingProcess doing the renames and its SHA256; encryption is already underway, so speed matters. Identify the scope (single share vs many hosts). 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host from the network, kill the encrypting process, disable the compromised account, and protect/segment backups and file shares before the encryptor reaches them. 3) Hunt: this actor also renames files with the victim's name as the extension on some segments, so also hunt for a sudden burst of files sharing one novel extension org-wide; back-trace to symantec.exe/g11.sys EDR-kill and AnyDesk footholds and check the qTox/email ransom note drop.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".God8Damn" or PreviousFileName endswith ".God8Damn"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FileName), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where FileCount >= 20   // 20 = mass-rename threshold to strip single-file noise
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".God8Damn" or TargetFileExtension =~ "God8Damn"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFileName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| where FileCount >= 20   // 20 = mass-rename threshold to strip single-file noise
| order by LastSeen desc
title: GodDamn Ransomware .God8Damn Encrypted File Extension

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

DeviceEvents

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or SHA1 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or MD5 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or SHA1 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or MD5 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Top AI Agents Built to Catch Malicious Code Can Be Tricked Into Running It

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 13 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Ask an AI coding agent to scan open-source code for security holes, and it might run the attacker's code on your own machine instead. That is the finding in a&nbsp;proof-of-concept published Wednesday&nbsp;by the AI Now Institute, an attack it calls "Friendly Fire." It works against Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex when either is running in an autonomous mode that approves its own

Poisoned repo drop: security.sh + disguised 'code_policies' Go binary on host AIDelivery High
Hunts the delivery step of the AI Now 'Friendly Fire' PoC: a third-party library that ships a security.sh wrapper alongside a pre-compiled 'code_policies' payload binary disguised as the build of a co-located code_policies.go decoy. Fires on creation of these specific artifacts (e.g. during git clone/checkout) before any AI agent runs them. Rationale: Anchors on the exact artifact names from the PoC repo (security.sh, code_policies, code_policies.go) confirmed by both the AI Now brief and the Boyan-MILANOV GitHub repo — code_policies/.go are near-unique strings, giving high fidelity for the drop before execution. Cross-checked against: • https://ainowinstitute.org/publications/friendly-fire-exploit-brief • https://github.com/Boyan-MILANOV/friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cyber-ai-agents-hijacked/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project that genuinely ships a helper file named security.sh (a fairly common CI/security-scan script name)
  • A researcher cloning the public stripped-payload PoC repo for reproduction
  • A Go project that legitimately contains a package/file named code_policies.go
  • Developer authoring their own security.sh linting wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit") and FileName == "code_policies.go")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect FolderPath/InitiatingProcess — confirm the write came from git/clone into an untrusted third-party repo and that a co-located code_policies binary (no extension, ELF/PE) sits beside code_policies.go. Hash the binary and check prevalence/VT. 2) Contain: quarantine the repo directory, block the code_policies SHA256, and prevent any AI coding agent from being pointed at that folder in auto mode. 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceProcessEvents for any execution of security.sh or code_policies on the host (UCs below) and for other repos on the same dev box carrying an unreferenced compiled binary next to a same-named .go source.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ ("security.sh","code_policies","code_policies.go","code_policies.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("security.sh","code_policies","code_policies.go","code_policies.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI coding agent (Claude Code / Codex) executing README-suggested security.sh AIExploitation High
Core Friendly Fire detection: an AI coding agent process (claude/codex/node) spawns the security.sh wrapper or the code_policies payload while auto-reviewing untrusted code — the agent runs a script that only a README told it to run, with no user approval. Parent-process pivot on the agent binary makes this a security-tool-executes-unexpected-code signal. Rationale: Combines the article's named artifacts (security.sh, code_policies) with the AI-agent parent process (claude/codex/node) — the exact 'the agent executing a binary or script that only a README told it to run' behaviour the researchers flag as the clearest thing to watch for. Cross-checked against: • https://ainowinstitute.org/publications/friendly-fire-exploit-brief • https://github.com/Boyan-MILANOV/friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher deliberately reproducing the (stripped) PoC with Claude Code / Codex
  • A legitimate repo whose own build/test flow the agent runs that happens to invoke a file named security.sh
  • Developer manually running security.sh in a shell that was itself launched by the agent's terminal integration
  • Internal tooling named code_policies used sanctioned in the org
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit" and AccountName !in~ ("secresearch","redteam")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm InitiatingProcessFileName is a real AI agent (claude/codex/node running the CLI) and that the target repo is untrusted third-party code, not an internal project; capture the code_policies SHA256 and FolderPath. 2) Contain: kill the agent process, isolate the host, block the binary hash, and disable auto-mode/auto-review for that workspace. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents from the code_policies process and its descendants for any egress (PoC stops at exec, but a real port may add C2), and sweep other dev endpoints for the same agent-parent → security.sh chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "security.sh" or ProcessCommandLine has "code_policies" or FileName in~ ("code_policies","code_policies.exe"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude","claude.exe","codex","codex.exe","node","node.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "security.sh" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "code_policies" or TargetProcessName has "code_policies")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("claude","codex","node")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Disguised 'code_policies' payload binary executed (masquerades as Go build) AIInstallation High
Fires on execution of the code_policies binary — the Friendly Fire payload carrier disguised as the compiled build of a co-located code_policies.go, seeded with strings lifted from that source so the agent's disassembly check ties them together. Surfaces the payload process, its hash, and parent (security.sh/shell) for IOC pivoting regardless of which agent launched it. Rationale: code_policies is the near-unique payload-binary name confirmed by the PoC repo; the masquerade (a compiled binary disguised as the build of code_policies.go, string-seeded to fool disassembly) is the defense-evasion crux, so any execution of it is high-fidelity and yields the hash for blocking. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/Boyan-MILANOV/friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cyber-ai-agents-hijacked/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1027 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate static-analysis tool genuinely named code_policies in the environment
  • Security team reproducing the public PoC (payload stripped) for validation
  • A build system compiling code_policies.go into a same-named binary in a sanctioned internal project
  • EDR sample-detonation of the artifact in a sandbox VM
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the code_policies SHA256/MD5 and FolderPath; confirm parent is security.sh/a shell under an AI agent and that no repo source actually references the binary (the tell — nothing calls it). 2) Contain: block the hash org-wide, isolate the host, and terminate the process tree. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts that have ever written or run code_policies, review child processes and outbound connections for post-exec activity, and check whether any secrets/keys on the dev host were accessed during the process lifetime.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "code_policies" or ProcessCommandLine has "code_policies" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "code_policies"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "code_policies" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "code_policies" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "code_policies"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Hash, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI coding agent executes a repo-local binary during autonomous review (Friendly Fire port) AIExploitation Medium
Behavioral generalization of Friendly Fire for real-world ports that rename the artifacts: an AI coding agent (claude/codex) in auto mode executes a compiled binary living inside a user code/repo directory that is not a standard toolchain interpreter — i.e. running a payload that only the repo's docs pointed it to. Hunting-tier because it drops the specific PoC names in favor of the behaviour. Rationale: The researchers say the payload ports to almost any project with different filenames, so this drops the PoC-specific names and keys on the invariant: an AI coding agent auto-executing a non-toolchain compiled binary from within an untrusted repo tree — the durable behaviour behind Friendly Fire. Cross-checked against: • https://ainowinstitute.org/publications/friendly-fire-exploit-brief • https://www.nxcode.io/resources/news/friendly-fire-rogue-agent-ai-coding-security-2026
ATT&CKT1059 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Agent legitimately running a project binary it just built (e.g. ./myapp, ./target/release/app) as part of a requested build-and-run task
  • Repo-local test harness or fuzzer binaries invoked by the agent during sanctioned work
  • Language servers or linters shipped inside a repo's tools/ directory
  • Monorepo task-runner binaries executed from the workspace root
  • Developer-blessed helper executables in Downloads used during triage
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("go build","cargo build","npm run build","make ") or FolderPath has_any (@"\target\release\", @"\target\debug\", @"\dist\", @"\build\", "/target/release/", "/dist/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the executed binary's SHA256, prevalence, and whether any repo source references it; confirm the agent was in auto-mode reviewing untrusted third-party code rather than building a trusted project. 2) Contain: if unrecognized/low-prevalence, isolate the host, block the hash, and switch the affected workspace to approve-before-run. 3) Hunt: baseline which binaries each agent normally executes per user, alert on first-seen repo-local executables, and correlate with README/docs files added in the same repo that instruct running a checker/script.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude","claude.exe","codex","codex.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Documents\", @"\repos\", @"\projects\", @"\src\", "/home/", "/Users/", "/tmp/")
| where FileName !in~ ("node","node.exe","npm","npm.cmd","git","git.exe","python","python3","python.exe","pip","pip3","go","cargo","rustc","tsc","jest","pytest","bash","bash.exe","sh","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","pwsh","powershell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("claude","codex")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("Downloads","Documents","repos","projects","/home/","/Users/","/tmp/","src")
| where not(TargetProcessName has_any ("node","npm","git","python","pip","cargo","rustc","tsc","jest","pytest","bash","sh","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\claude.exe OR *\\Claude.exe OR *\\codex.exe OR *\\Codex.exe) @Image:(*\\Downloads\\* OR *\\Documents\\* OR *\\repos\\* OR *\\projects\\* OR *\\src\\*) -@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.cmd OR *\\git.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\pip.exe OR *\\go.exe OR *\\cargo.exe OR *\\bash.exe OR *\\sh.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(claude|codex)(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(Downloads|Documents|repos|projects|src|tmp)(\\|\/)/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/(node|npm|git|python[0-9]?|pip[0-9]?|go|cargo|rustc|tsc|jest|pytest|bash|sh|dash|zsh|cmd|powershell|pwsh)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="claude" OR Processes.parent_process_name="claude.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="codex" OR Processes.parent_process_name="codex.exe") (Processes.process_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Documents\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*/repos/*" OR Processes.process_path="*/projects/*" OR Processes.process_path="*/home/*" OR Processes.process_path="*/Users/*") NOT (Processes.process_name IN ("node","node.exe","npm","git","git.exe","python","python3","pip","go","cargo","bash","sh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39861")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39861")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-39861")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-39861")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution

status: experimental
description: |

    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

GhostApproval Symlink Flaws Could Let Malicious Repos Run Code in AI Coding Agents

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 11 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers at&nbsp;Wiz&nbsp;found that a flaw in six popular AI coding assistants lets a booby-trapped code project quietly take control of a developer's computer. The assistant asks permission to edit one harmless-looking file, but the write lands on a sensitive one instead. The affected tools are Amazon Q Developer, Anthropic's Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf.

CVEsCVE-2026-12958 CVE-2026-50549 CVE-2026-12957
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1555.003

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Symlink created in repo pointing to SSH/AWS/shell files (GhostApproval staging)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Amazon Q / AI agent spawns shell child from poisoned .amazonq/mcp.json (CVE-2026-12957) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] AI coding agent writes SSH authorized_keys or shell rc via GhostApproval symlink · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SSH authorized_keys planted then remote SSH logon (GhostApproval key-injection use) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
AI coding agent writes SSH authorized_keys or shell rc via GhostApproval symlink AIInstallation High
Hunts the GhostApproval payload landing: an AI coding assistant process (Amazon Q, Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Augment, Antigravity) creating or modifying ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or a shell startup file (~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc, ~/.profile) because a repo symlink named like a benign config file (project_settings.json) resolved to the sensitive target. This is the write that grants password-less SSH or arbitrary command execution on the next terminal. Rationale: Anchored on the exact GhostApproval targets confirmed by Wiz (~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.zshrc) and the six named agent processes; the pairing of a sensitive Unix dotfile write with an AI-agent initiating process is the specific, high-fidelity signal the article describes. Cross-checked Wiz blog and AWS bulletin. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/ghostapproval-a-trust-boundary-gap-in-ai-coding-assistants • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/2026-047-aws/
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1546.004 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • nvm / oh-my-zsh / starship installers spawned via node appending to ~/.zshrc during legit setup
  • A developer intentionally letting an agent add its own SSH key to authorized_keys for a remote dev container
  • Dotfile-manager tooling (chezmoi, yadm) launched from an IDE-embedded terminal running under node
  • Python-based provisioning scripts (Ansible local, pip post-install hooks) editing ~/.bashrc
  • IDE 'shell integration' features writing rc-file hooks on first launch
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("oh-my-zsh","nvm.sh","chezmoi","yadm","starship init") and FileName in~ (".zshrc",".bashrc"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the parent repo path; open the target file and diff — a foreign ssh-rsa/ed25519 key in authorized_keys or an exported command / curl|bash line in .zshrc confirms it. Check whether the workspace was a freshly cloned/untrusted repo. 2) CONTAIN: Remove the injected key/line, rotate any exposed SSH keys, revoke the developer's active sessions, and quarantine the repo. If SSH is internet-reachable, block the host at the firewall until cleaned. 3) HUNT: Search all endpoints for the same agent process writing dotfiles; pivot to remote SSH logons on the host after the write and to any .amazonq/mcp.json in the repo.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName == "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh/")
    or FileName in~ (".zshrc",".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshenv",".zprofile",".zlogin")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","code","Code.exe","cursor","Cursor","cursor.exe","windsurf","Windsurf","windsurf.exe","claude","antigravity","augment","python","python3")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("amazonq","amazon-q","language-server","cursor","windsurf","claude","augment","antigravity")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ssh-keygen","sshd"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (TargetFileName == "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh/")
    or TargetFileName in~ (".zshrc",".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshenv",".zprofile",".zlogin")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","code","cursor","windsurf","claude","antigravity","augment")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("amazonq","language-server","cursor","windsurf","claude","augment","antigravity")
| where ActingProcessName !has "ssh-keygen"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Amazon Q / AI agent spawns shell child from poisoned .amazonq/mcp.json (CVE-2026-12957) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-12957: a poisoned repo ships an .amazonq/mcp.json (or equivalent agent config) that Amazon Q auto-loads once the workspace is trusted, launching MCP-server processes that inherit the developer's AWS keys and can run commands. Detects an AI agent / language-server process spawning a shell or interpreter child that runs credential-touching commands (curl, chmod, base64, reads of ~/.aws). Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit CVE-2026-12957 detail (poisoned repo auto-loads a config file .amazonq/mcp.json and runs commands to steal AWS keys) plus the six named agent parents; requires the agent->shell->credential-command chain rather than bare agent-spawns-node so it stays hunting-grade. Cross-checked AWS bulletin 2026-047 and Wiz. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/2026-047-aws/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/amazon-q-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1195.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate MCP server defined by a trusted repo shelling out to curl/pip during normal setup
  • Language-server post-install hooks running python/base64 for packaging
  • Developer-authored VS Code tasks that chmod +x build scripts
  • AI agent legitimately fetching a dependency via curl during a user-approved build
  • CI-runner style repos where node spawns bash for test bootstrap
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/build/","npm run","pytest","pip install") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","npm") and not ProcessCommandLine has_any (".aws/credentials","authorized_keys"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full ProcessCommandLine of the shell child and inspect the repo for .amazonq/mcp.json (or similar agent config) with an unexpected 'command'/'args'. Confirm whether ~/.aws/credentials was read or exfiltrated (network egress from the child). 2) CONTAIN: Kill the spawned process tree, rotate the developer's AWS keys and any cloud CLI tokens immediately, and revoke sessions. Update Amazon Q Language Server to >=1.69.0. 3) HUNT: Enumerate repos on the host for agent config files (.amazonq/mcp.json, mcp.json), review DeviceNetworkEvents from the agent for uploads to unfamiliar hosts, and check for the SSH-key / dotfile writes from the companion UCs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","code","Code.exe","cursor","Cursor","cursor.exe","windsurf","Windsurf","windsurf.exe","claude","antigravity","augment")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("amazonq","amazon-q","language-server",".amazonq/mcp.json","mcp.json")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","dash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","python","python3","osascript")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","chmod","base64",".aws/credentials",".aws\\credentials","authorized_keys","aws_access_key")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "mcp.json"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","code","cursor","windsurf","claude","antigravity","augment")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("amazonq","language-server","mcp.json")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("bash","/sh","zsh","dash","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","python","osascript")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","chmod","base64",".aws/credentials","authorized_keys","aws_access_key")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has "mcp.json"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
