SSH authorized_keys planted then remote SSH logon (GhostApproval key-injection use) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Temporal correlation that catches the payoff of the GhostApproval SSH variant: ~/.ssh/authorized_keys is created/modified on a host, then a successful remote (network/SSH) logon occurs on the same host within an hour using the freshly planted key. Distinguishes a benign key add from an attacker immediately logging in. Rationale: Chains the two article-confirmed facts (agent writes into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, then 'they can log in with no password') into a time-window correlation so it only fires when the planted key is actually used remotely - far tighter than alerting on every authorized_keys edit. Corroborated by Wiz PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/ghostapproval-a-trust-boundary-gap-in-ai-coding-assistants
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1021.004 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin adds a legitimate key then immediately SSHes in to validate access
  • Configuration-management (Ansible/Salt) pushing authorized_keys followed by a scripted SSH health check
  • Cloud-init / provisioning that installs a key then the orchestrator connects
  • Jump-host onboarding where a new key and first login happen back to back
  • Backup/CI service accounts rotating keys and reconnecting
Suppression filter
| where KeyWriter !in~ ("sshd","cloud-init","ansible","salt-minion","puppet","cfn-init")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the process that wrote authorized_keys is an AI agent (KeyWriter field) rather than sshd/cloud-init/config-mgmt, and check whether the RemoteIP of the logon is expected for that user. 2) CONTAIN: If unexpected, kill the SSH session, remove the injected key, rotate credentials, and block the source IP; isolate the host if the repo is confirmed malicious. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the RemoteIP across the fleet for other SSH logons, review commands run in the session, and search other hosts for the same agent writing authorized_keys or .zshrc.
let win = 1h;
let keyWrites = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where FileName == "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh/"
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
    | project KeyWriteTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where LogonType in ("Network","RemoteInteractive") or Protocol =~ "Ssh"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| join kind=inner keyWrites on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (KeyWriteTime .. KeyWriteTime + win)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, KeyWriteTime)
| project KeyWriteTime, LogonTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, RemoteIP, DelaySec, KeyWriter = InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LogonTime desc
let win = 1h;
let keyWrites = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where TargetFileName == "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh/"
    | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
    | project KeyWriteTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ProcessName == "sshd" and SyslogMessage has "Accepted publickey"
| join kind=inner keyWrites on $left.Computer == $right.DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (KeyWriteTime .. KeyWriteTime + win)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, KeyWriteTime)
| project KeyWriteTime, LogonTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, SyslogMessage, DelaySec, ActingProcessName
| order by LogonTime desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:sshd "Accepted publickey"
#event_simpleName=UserLogon
| RemoteAddressIP4=*
| LogonType=/(3|10)/
| join({#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\/\.ssh\/authorized_keys$/i | rename(ContextImageFileName, as=KeyWriter)}, field=aid, include=[KeyWriter])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, RemoteAddressIP4, KeyWriter], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as KeyWriteTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="authorized_keys" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/*" AND (Filesystem.action=created OR Filesystem.action=modified) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=inner dest [| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as LogonTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success AND (Authentication.app="sshd" OR Authentication.signature="ssh") by Authentication.dest Authentication.src Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`] | where LogonTime >= KeyWriteTime AND LogonTime <= KeyWriteTime+3600 | eval DelaySec=LogonTime-KeyWriteTime | convert ctime(KeyWriteTime) ctime(LogonTime) | table dest process_name KeyWriteTime LogonTime DelaySec src user
| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as KeyWriteTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="authorized_keys" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/*" AND (Filesystem.action=created OR Filesystem.action=modified) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=inner dest [| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as LogonTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success AND (Authentication.app="sshd" OR Authentication.signature="ssh") by Authentication.dest Authentication.src Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`] | where LogonTime >= KeyWriteTime AND LogonTime <= KeyWriteTime+3600 | eval DelaySec=LogonTime-KeyWriteTime | convert ctime(KeyWriteTime) ctime(LogonTime) | table dest process_name KeyWriteTime LogonTime DelaySec src user
Symlink created in repo pointing to SSH/AWS/shell files (GhostApproval staging) AIWeaponization Low
Hunts the GhostApproval staging step: creation of a symbolic link (ln -s, mklink, New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink) whose link name masquerades as a benign project file (e.g. project_settings.json) but whose target is a sensitive out-of-repo path (~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.zshrc, ~/.aws/credentials, /etc). Catches attacker/CI/manual symlink planting; note git-checkout creates symlinks via syscall and is not covered by process telemetry. Rationale: Anchored on the exact PoC command Wiz published (ln -s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys project_settings.json) and the confirmed sensitive targets; requires the symlink target to be a sensitive out-of-repo path so it does not fire on ordinary symlinks. Low confidence flagged because git checkout plants symlinks via syscall (not ln) and won't appear here - it complements, not replaces, the file-write UC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/ghostapproval-a-trust-boundary-gap-in-ai-coding-assistants
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dotfile managers (chezmoi, stow, yadm) that symlink ~/.zshrc or ~/.ssh/config into a managed repo
  • Developer manually symlinking a shared .env or config into a project
  • Build scripts that symlink /etc/localtime or CA bundles into a container context
  • Homebrew/Nix post-install linking into the user profile
  • Test fixtures that create relative parent-traversal symlinks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chezmoi","stow","yadm","nix","brew") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Resolve the symlink target vs its name (readlink) and confirm the link name looks like an in-repo config (e.g. *.json/.env) while the target is a sensitive dotfile - a mismatch is the GhostApproval tell. Check the repo origin/trust. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the symlink before any agent 'sets up' the repo, and if an agent already ran, inspect the target file for injected content and remediate per the SSH/rc UC. 3) HUNT: Grep the repo tree for other symlinks resolving outside the workspace, and search the fleet for the same repo/URL and for agent processes writing authorized_keys/.zshrc.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "ln" and ProcessCommandLine has "-s")
    or (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "mklink")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh") and ProcessCommandLine has "SymbolicLink")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("authorized_keys","/.ssh",".zshrc",".bashrc",".bash_profile",".aws","/etc/","System32","..\\..","../..")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (TargetProcessName endswith "/ln" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "-s")
    or (TargetProcessName has "cmd.exe" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "mklink")
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("powershell","pwsh") and TargetProcessCommandLine has "SymbolicLink")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("authorized_keys","/.ssh",".zshrc",".bashrc",".aws","/etc/","System32","..\\..","../..")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Symlink Created Pointing to SSH/AWS/Shell Files (GhostApproval Staging)
id: 4a71e2c5-0d3b-4f19-a6c2-7b8e9f014d22
status: experimental
description: Detects creation of a symbolic link whose target is a sensitive out-of-repo path, the GhostApproval symlink staging step.
references:
    - https://www.wiz.io/blog/ghostapproval-a-trust-boundary-gap-in-ai-coding-assistants
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ghostapproval-symlink-flaws-could-let.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:
    - attack.defense_evasion
    - attack.t1036.005
    - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: linux
detection:
    selection_ln:
        Image|endswith: '/ln'
        CommandLine|contains: '-s'
    selection_target:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'authorized_keys'
            - '/.ssh'
            - '.zshrc'
            - '.bashrc'
            - '.aws'
            - '/etc/'
    condition: selection_ln and selection_target
falsepositives:
    - Dotfile managers or setup scripts that symlink ~/.zshrc or ~/.ssh/config into a repo intentionally
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:ln AND @process.command_line:*"-s"* AND @process.command_line:(*authorized_keys* OR *.zshrc* OR *.bashrc* OR *.ssh* OR *.aws* OR */etc/*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\/ln$/i
| regex("\\s-s(\\s|f)", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(authorized_keys|/\\.ssh|\\.zshrc|\\.bashrc|\\.aws|/etc/|System32|\\.\\.)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="ln" AND Processes.process="*-s*") OR (Processes.process="*mklink*") OR (Processes.process="*SymbolicLink*")) AND (Processes.process="*authorized_keys*" OR Processes.process="*/.ssh*" OR Processes.process="*.zshrc*" OR Processes.process="*.bashrc*" OR Processes.process="*.aws*" OR Processes.process="*/etc/*" OR Processes.process="*System32*" OR Processes.process="*..*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="ln" AND Processes.process="*-s*") OR (Processes.process="*mklink*") OR (Processes.process="*SymbolicLink*")) AND (Processes.process="*authorized_keys*" OR Processes.process="*/.ssh*" OR Processes.process="*.zshrc*" OR Processes.process="*.bashrc*" OR Processes.process="*.aws*" OR Processes.process="*/etc/*" OR Processes.process="*System32*" OR Processes.process="*..*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents

ImFileEvent

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-12958", "CVE-2026-50549", "CVE-2026-12957")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-12958", "CVE-2026-50549", "CVE-2026-12957")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

Fake 7-Zip Installers Turn Devices Into Residential Proxy Nodes

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 12 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new threat actor dubbed Lurking Lizard that has been operating an end-to-end malicious residential proxy business using an infrastructure comprising more than 230 lookalike domains. The activity dates back to at least August 2022, according to DNS threat intelligence firm Infoblox. One such campaign, observed earlier this year, involved the

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Lurking Lizard proxyware lookalike distribution/proxy-brand domain resolution · [LLM] Fake installer (7-Zip/WhatsApp/WireVPN) written to disk from Lurking Lizard domain
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanized 7-Zip/WireVPN installer spawning command interpreter or LOLBin · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] IPLogger tracking beacon (iplogger.com/mnWD) from non-browser process · [LLM] Residential-proxy client check-in to /client_v1/config/http and /client_v1/version/server · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Lurking Lizard proxyware lookalike distribution/proxy-brand domain resolution AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS resolution and network connections to the Lurking Lizard lookalike domains used to distribute trojanized 7-Zip/WhatsApp/WireVPN installers and to impersonate proxy brands. Article-specific because it pins the exact drop-catch/typosquat domains (7zip.com vs 7-zip.org, whtatsapp.net, wirevpn.*) rather than a generic newly-registered-domain heuristic. Rationale: Uses the exact Infoblox-published typosquat/drop-catch domains (7zip.com not 7-zip.org, whtatsapp.net, wirevpn.app/.cc/.io) plus the impersonated proxy-brand domains — a fixed IOC list, so any resolution is high-fidelity rather than a generic NRD heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/fake-installers-fake-reviews-fake-services-real-proxies-real-victims/ • https://gbhackers.com/lurking-lizard-uses-drop-catch-domains/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/lurking-lizard-uses-fake-7-zip-installers/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst detonating/browsing the reported domains from a sandbox VM
  • URL-detonation or web-crawler appliance fetching the domains for reputation scoring
  • User genuinely searching for '911proxy'/'smartproxy' proxy services and landing on the lookalike storefront
  • DNS sinkhole/passive-DNS collector resolving the domains as part of enrichment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on DeviceName/src — was resolution followed by an .exe/.msi download from the same host? Check InitiatingProcessFileName (browser vs. non-browser). 2) Contain: block the domains at DNS/proxy, isolate the host if a non-browser process resolved them or an installer was written. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the same domains, check for iplogger.com/mnWD beacons and /client_v1/* proxy check-ins (UC2/UC3), and enumerate installers dropped from these hosts.

| where RemoteUrl has_any ("7zip.com","whtatsapp.net","wirevpn.app","wirevpn.cc","wirevpn.io","snaptik.io","isharkvpn.com","betflixfree.net","smartproxy.org","ipidea.org","911proxy.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort

IPLogger tracking beacon (iplogger.com/mnWD) from non-browser process AICommand & Control High
Hunts the hardcoded IPLogger tracking link (iplogger.com/mnWD) embedded in the Lurking Lizard fake-installer samples, contacted by a non-browser process. Article-specific: this exact IPLogger short-URL is the single artifact Infoblox used to tie the 7-Zip, TikTok/YouTube-downloader and WireVPN samples to the same actor. Rationale: iplogger.com/mnWD is the specific tracking artifact Infoblox names as the pivot linking every fake-installer variant to Lurking Lizard; contact from a non-browser process is a strong proxyware-beacon signal, and the /mnWD path (in proxy/web logs) makes it campaign-unique rather than generic IPLogger noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/fake-installers-fake-reviews-fake-services-real-proxies-real-victims/ • https://gbhackers.com/lurking-lizard-uses-drop-catch-domains/
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate marketing/analytics use of IPLogger by an internal user clicking a tracked link in a browser (excluded by the non-browser filter)
  • Security tooling detonating a sample and following the embedded IPLogger link
  • Chat/IM client following a user-pasted iplogger.com link
  • Threat-intel enrichment service resolving iplogger.com for reputation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is not a browser and inspect its folder path (Downloads/Temp/AppData) and parent — a fresh installer beaconing to IPLogger is the trojanized dropper. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture the beaconing binary + hash, block iplogger.com/mnWD at proxy. 3) Hunt: pull the binary's other network destinations (proxy /client_v1/* endpoints, UC3), check autoruns/scheduled tasks for persistence, and search the org for the same SHA256.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl contains "iplogger.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","safari.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "iplogger.com/mnWD" or DstHostname =~ "iplogger.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, HttpMethod, Url, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Residential-proxy client check-in to /client_v1/config/http and /client_v1/version/server AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Lurking Lizard proxyware client's HTTP check-in to its config/version API endpoints, which Infoblox found shared identical schemas across the campaign's domains. Article-specific: these exact URI paths are the proxy client's C2/registration channel that turns the host into an exit node. Rationale: The /client_v1/config/http and /client_v1/version/server paths are the campaign-specific API schema Infoblox observed across multiple Lurking Lizard domains — an unusual, non-standard URI pair unlikely to collide with legitimate traffic. Datadog/Falcon left blank because HTTP URI paths are not reliably present in Sysmon-only or FDR EDR telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/fake-installers-fake-reviews-fake-services-real-proxies-real-victims/ • https://gbhackers.com/lurking-lizard-uses-drop-catch-domains/
ATT&CKT1090 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal API that happens to expose a /client_v1/version/server versioning path (verify destination host is external/untrusted)
  • Web-app pentest or fuzzing traffic hitting versioned API paths
  • Vulnerability scanner probing common API routes
  • Proxy log parsing that URL-decodes and matches a similarly named path on a trusted SaaS host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination host is external and matches (or resolves like) the Lurking Lizard lookalike infra; identify the source process/host and its install origin. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the destination and the /client_v1/* paths at proxy, kill/quarantine the proxy client binary. 3) Hunt: this host is likely an active exit node — review outbound volume for third-party proxied traffic, correlate with the iplogger beacon (UC2) and installer drop (UC4), and sweep peers for the same URI paths.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/client_v1/config/http","/client_v1/version/server")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any ("/client_v1/config/http","/client_v1/version/server")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, HttpMethod, Url, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake installer (7-Zip/WhatsApp/WireVPN) written to disk from Lurking Lizard domain AIDelivery High
Hunts an executable/MSI installer written to disk whose download origin is a Lurking Lizard lookalike domain, catching the trojanized 7-Zip/WhatsApp/WireVPN/Snaptik installer at the delivery step. Article-specific via the concrete distribution domains plus the impersonated product names. Rationale: Combines the named distribution domains with an executable/MSI file-origin — Defender's FileOriginUrl ties the dropped installer directly to the actor's infra. Sigma/Datadog/Falcon blank: the FileOriginUrl-to-file correlation has no clean single-event Sigma shape and no FDR/Sysmon file-origin equivalent, so Splunk/Sentinel use the web-download view instead. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/fake-installers-fake-reviews-fake-services-real-proxies-real-victims/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/lurking-lizard-uses-fake-7-zip-installers/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst intentionally downloading a sample from the reported domain for analysis
  • URL-rewrite/email-security gateway pre-fetching a linked installer
  • Browser 'download and scan' feature retrieving the file into a sandbox
  • Web proxy caching an .exe from the flagged host during content inspection
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the dropped file SHA256 and confirm it is NOT the legitimate Igor Pavlov 7-Zip (compare against official 7-zip.org hashes); check if it was executed. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block the origin domain, isolate the host if the installer ran. 3) Hunt: if executed, look for the IPLogger beacon (UC2), the /client_v1/* proxy check-in (UC3) and child-process spawns (UC5); sweep the org for the same SHA256 and origin domains.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileOriginUrl has_any ("7zip.com","whtatsapp.net","wirevpn.app","wirevpn.cc","wirevpn.io","snaptik.io","isharkvpn.com","betflixfree.net")
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".msi"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

Trojanized 7-Zip/WireVPN installer spawning command interpreter or LOLBin AIInstallation Low
Behavioral hunt for a 7-Zip/WireVPN/Snaptik installer-named parent process spawning cmd/PowerShell/mshta/rundll32/regsvr32/wscript — the execution of the hidden proxy payload bundled in the trojanized installer. Legitimate 7-Zip (7z/7zFM/7zG) rarely spawns interpreters, making this a useful low-noise pivot. Rationale: Anchors on the article's installer product names (7-Zip, WireVPN, Snaptik, iSharkVPN) as the parent and standard interpreters/LOLBins as the child; genuine 7-Zip archive tools almost never spawn these, so the parent-child pair is the intent signal. Low confidence because the article does not name the specific payload binary, so this is a hunting pivot rather than a hard IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/fake-installers-fake-reviews-fake-services-real-proxies-real-victims/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/lurking-lizard-uses-fake-7-zip-installers/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 7-Zip SFX/self-extracting archive that runs a bundled setup.cmd/install script
  • Software packaging or IT deployment wrapping 7-Zip to launch cmd/PowerShell post-extract
  • WhatsApp desktop updater spawning a helper process
  • A build/CI agent using 7z.exe in a pipeline that then calls cmd.exe
  • Legitimate WireVPN client (if org uses one) invoking rundll32 for driver setup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\") and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("MpCmdRun","DismHost","choco"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line for download/execution (curl/certutil/bitsadmin, base64, or connections) and confirm the parent is a downloaded installer, not a signed 7-zip.org build. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the installer + child artifacts, capture hashes. 3) Hunt: verify network for iplogger.com/mnWD (UC2) and /client_v1/* proxy check-ins (UC3), check Run keys/Scheduled Tasks for persistence of the proxy client, and sweep peers for the same parent binary hash.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("7z","7zip","7-zip","wirevpn","snaptik","isharkvpn","whatsapp")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("7z","7zip","7-zip","wirevpn","snaptik","isharkvpn","whatsapp")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fake 7-Zip/WireVPN Installer Spawning Interpreter or LOLBin
id: 4d0b8e5c-3f19-4a7d-9b62-1c8a7e2f60b9
status: experimental
description: Detects a 7-Zip/WireVPN/Snaptik installer-named parent process spawning a command interpreter or LOLBin, indicative of a trojanized Lurking Lizard installer executing its hidden proxy payload.
references:
  - https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/fake-installers-fake-reviews-fake-services-real-proxies-real-victims/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fake-7-zip-installers-turn-devices-into.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\7z.exe'
      - '\7zFM.exe'
      - '\7zG.exe'
      - '\7zip.exe'
      - '\wirevpn.exe'
      - '\snaptik.exe'
      - '\isharkvpn.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\7z.exe OR *\\7zFM.exe OR *\\7zG.exe OR *\\7zip.exe OR *\\wirevpn.exe OR *\\WireVPN.exe OR *\\snaptik.exe OR *\\isharkvpn.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(7z|7zFM|7zG|7zip|7-zip|wirevpn|snaptik|isharkvpn).*\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|wscript|cscript|curl|bitsadmin|certutil)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("7z.exe","7zFM.exe","7zG.exe","7zip.exe","7-zip.exe","wirevpn.exe","snaptik.exe","isharkvpn.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*7-zip*setup*" OR Processes.parent_process="*wirevpn*setup*" OR Processes.parent_process="*snaptik*setup*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("7z.exe","7zFM.exe","7zG.exe","7zip.exe","7-zip.exe","wirevpn.exe","snaptik.exe","isharkvpn.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*7-zip*setup*" OR Processes.parent_process="*wirevpn*setup*" OR Processes.parent_process="*snaptik*setup*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)

Snyk
2026-07-09 5 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A harmless-looking symlink in a Git repo can redirect a tool into reading or writing anywhere on your machine. That old trick is now showing up in AI coding assistants, with nasty results.

CVEsCVE-2026-12958 CVE-2026-50549 CVE-2024-32002 CVE-2024-21626 CVE-2021-32803
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Git-spawned hook execution during recursive clone (CVE-2024-32002) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SSH authorized_keys written by non-SSH tooling (symlink repo payload) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SSH authorized_keys written by non-SSH tooling (symlink repo payload) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes/modifications to any user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys where the writing process is NOT legitimate SSH provisioning tooling — the payoff of the article's headline attack, where a symlink named like project_settings.json checked out from a cloned repo resolves to authorized_keys and a build script/editor/AI coding agent silently writes an attacker key through it. Because the OS resolves the symlink transparently, the file event reports the real target path (.ssh/authorized_keys), which is the tell. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact payload path ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (code Block 1) written by non-SSH tooling — the symlink resolves so the OS reports the real target, making the write-through observable. Cross-checked MITRE T1098.004, Splunk Security Content and Elastic authorized_keys rules to confirm the technique and avoid duplicating a generic FIM rule by scoping on the writing process. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004/ • https://research.splunk.com/endpoint/f5ab595e-28e5-4327-8077-5008ba97c850/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/cross-platform/persistence_ssh_authorized_keys_modification
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Puppet/Salt/Terraform pushing authorized_keys via a config-management run (excluded, but custom wrappers may slip through)
  • Developer legitimately running ssh-copy-id or manually editing authorized_keys with vim/nano
  • Cloud-init / provisioning agent seeding keys on first boot of a new VM
  • CI runner injecting a deploy key into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as an intended step
  • Dotfile-management tools (chezmoi, GNU stow) that symlink or template SSH config
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("terraform","authorized_keys_command","chezmoi","stow") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess chain — is the writer a dev tool (git, node, python, code, cursor) or shell spawned from a freshly cloned repo path? Compare the written key fingerprint against the user's known keys and check if the file is/was a symlink (ls -l ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, readlink). 2) Contain: if the key is unrecognized, remove the offending authorized_keys line, kill active sessions authenticated by it, and rotate the account; quarantine the source repo. 3) Hunt: search the same host/user for the source symlink (git ls-files -s | grep '^120000'), other writes to ~/.ssh, ~/.bashrc, ~/.git/hooks, and any inbound SSH logons using the added key.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (FileName == "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sshd","ssh","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","useradd","adduser","ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFilePath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (TargetFileName == "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("sshd","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","ansible","puppet","salt-minion"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SSH authorized_keys Written by Non-SSH Tooling (Symlink Repo Payload)
id: 5c2e6b1a-9f3d-4a77-8b0e-2d1c6f9a4e21
description: Detects creation or modification of a user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys by a process that is not legitimate SSH provisioning tooling, consistent with a symlink committed to a cloned git repository resolving to authorized_keys and being written through by a build script, editor, or AI coding agent.
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/symlinks-are-still-scary/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1098.004
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '/.ssh/authorized_keys'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sshd'
      - '/ssh-keygen'
      - '/ssh-copy-id'
      - '/cloud-init'
      - '/ansible'
      - '/salt-minion'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*authorized_keys* AND (*">>"* OR *tee* OR *">"*)) -@process.executable.path:(*/sshd OR */ssh-keygen OR */ssh-copy-id OR */cloud-init)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\/\.ssh\/authorized_keys$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\/(sshd|ssh-keygen|ssh-copy-id|cloud-init)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/authorized_keys" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified","renamed") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_guid
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/authorized_keys" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified","renamed") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_guid
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Git-spawned hook execution during recursive clone (CVE-2024-32002) AIExploitation High
Hunts a process whose image lives inside a .git/hooks/ directory and whose parent is git — the exact signature of CVE-2024-32002, where a malicious repository's crafted submodule + symlink writes a hook into .git/ that git executes while the clone is still running, yielding RCE from nothing more than git clone --recurse-submodules. No build step or 'run the project' required. Rationale: Anchored on the CVE-2024-32002 mechanic named in the article (git clone --recurse-submodules dropping a script into .git/hooks and running it during clone). The parent=git + child-image-in-.git/hooks pair is high-fidelity because hooks are not supposed to execute during a clone; confirmed via the git security advisory GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv and Amal Murali's PoC writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/git/git/security/advisories/GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv • https://amalmurali.me/posts/git-rce/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2024/05/16/git-cve-2024-32002/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer with legitimately installed local git hooks (post-checkout/post-merge) firing during a normal pull or checkout
  • Husky / pre-commit framework hooks that shell out during commit or checkout operations
  • CI systems that intentionally invoke repo hooks as part of a pipeline stage
  • git-lfs post-checkout smudge hooks running on a large-file repo clone
  • Monorepo tooling (e.g. Nx, Turborepo) that registers checkout hooks
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("husky","git-lfs","post-merge") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pull","checkout HEAD","lfs"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the executed hook file under .git/hooks/ and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm it was a clone/--recurse-submodules op and read the hook body for network callbacks or key writes. Check git version on host against the patched set (>=2.39.4/2.40.2/2.41.1/2.42.2/2.43.4/2.44.1/2.45.1). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the hook process tree, and quarantine the cloned repo directory; block the source repo URL. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for downstream child processes of the hook, writes to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, new persistence (cron, systemd units, shell rc files), and outbound C2 from the hook's PID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.git/hooks/", "\\.git\\hooks\\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","git.exe","git-remote-https","git-remote-https.exe","bash","sh","dash")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","submodule","--recurse-submodules") or FolderPath has_any ("post-checkout","post-clone","post-update")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/.git/hooks/", "\\.git\\hooks\\")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("git","bash","sh","dash")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","submodule","--recurse-submodules") or ActingProcessName has_any ("post-checkout","post-clone","post-update")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joro proxy-mode confused-deputy: browser POSTs to loopback API 127.0.0.1:9090 (CVE-2026-53649) AIDelivery Low
Hunts a web browser process opening connections to the Joro proxy-mode API on loopback TCP/9090, the confused-deputy vector CVE-2026-53649 abuses when attacker-controlled cross-origin JavaScript reaches the unauthenticated, wildcard-CORS Joro API. Article-specific because it pins the exact bind (127.0.0.1:9090) and the browser-mediated initiator. Rationale: Uses the exact loopback bind (127.0.0.1:9090) named in the advisory plus a browser-process initiator, the confused-deputy shape of CVE-2026-53649. Deliberately hunting/Low because a legitimate Joro operator's own browser talks to the same UI/API port. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling • https://github.com/bishopfox
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Joro operator using the proxy-mode web UI, which itself talks to 127.0.0.1:9090
  • Unrelated local dev services on 9090 (Prometheus Pushgateway, SonarQube, custom app) that a browser hits
  • Browser DevTools/extension polling a localhost dev server on the same port
  • Local reverse-proxy or API mock bound to 9090 during development
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Joro is installed/running on the host and whether the operator was actively using the Joro UI at that timestamp; pull the browser history for the immediately preceding external navigation. 2) Contain: if the loopback hit was NOT operator-initiated UI use, kill the joro process, isolate the host, and block the external page's domain at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot to whether joro subsequently wrote a .so plugin, restarted, or spawned an interactive shell (see companion UCs) — that sequence confirms exploitation.

| where RemotePort == 9090
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("firefox","firefox-bin","chrome","chromium","msedge","brave","Google Chrome","Firefox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc

Joro native plugin RCE: joro process spawns interactive /bin/bash shell (CVE-2026-53649) AIExploitation High
Alerts when the joro binary spawns an interactive Unix shell (bash/sh/dash/zsh with -i), the terminal step of the CVE-2026-53649 chain where a malicious uploaded plugin's init() opens a goroutine and yields an interactive /bin/bash -i shell as the operator's user. High fidelity because joro is a proxy/teamserver, not a shell launcher — it has no legitimate reason to fork a local login shell. Rationale: Pins the article's exact parent (joro) and payload (interactive /bin/bash -i obtained on plugin.Open() init()). Because Joro is a proxy that never legitimately forks a local login shell, parent=joro + shell + -i is a near-zero-FP RCE tell. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.004 T1129
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Joro developer/operator debugging the tool and manually shelling out from a plugin during testing
  • A local wrapper or helper script also named 'joro' that legitimately invokes a shell
  • Operator running a benign self-authored plugin that spawns a shell for tooling
  • CI/build harness building Joro plugins that exec a shell as part of a test
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child shell's full process tree and any sockets it holds (ss -p); confirm the joro process previously loaded a newly-written .so and restarted. 2) Contain: kill the shell and joro process, isolate the host, and snapshot /proc for the joro PID before termination for the loaded-plugin path. 3) Hunt: enumerate the Joro plugin directory for attacker-uploaded .so files, review recent POSTs to /api/v1/plugins/upload and /api/v1/system/restart, and check outbound connections from joro to external hosts.

| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-i"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "-i"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joro writes a native .so plugin: attacker plugin drop before restart (CVE-2026-53649) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the joro process writing a shared-object (.so) plugin file to disk, the staging step where CVE-2026-53649's unauthenticated upload endpoint persists an attacker-supplied native plugin that executes its init() on the next plugin.Open(). Article-specific via the joro-process writer plus the .so plugin artifact. Rationale: Ties the article's plugin-upload artifact (a native .so consumed by plugin.Open()) to the joro process as writer. joro dropping a .so it did not build interactively is the on-disk footprint of the upload endpoint being abused. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin"

Nuclio CronJob curl shell-injection reading Kubernetes serviceaccount token AIExploitation High
Hunts a /bin/sh -c curl invocation (as built by the Nuclio controller for cron triggers) whose command line both reads the pod serviceaccount token and contains shell metacharacters, indicating exploitation of CVE-2026-52831 header-key/body command injection. Article-specific because it pins on the exact curl --header shape plus the /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token read shown in the PoC. Rationale: Anchors on the exact PoC artefacts: a curl --header command line (the controller's generated sink) that also reads /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, plus shell metacharacters ($(, ;, &&) that only appear when Path-A/Path-B injection breaks the quoting context.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator running kubectl exec into a pod and using curl -H with the serviceaccount token to test the Kubernetes API
  • Legitimate in-cluster script that curls the API server with a custom header whose value contains '; charset=utf-8'
  • CIS-benchmark / security scanner tooling that reads the serviceaccount token path
  • CI/CD sidecar that reads the token and curls an internal admission endpoint
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine contains "; charset=" or ProcessCommandLine contains ";q=" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "kubectl")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and confirm the injected fragment (text after the closing quote of --header, or a $(...) in the echoed body); map the host/pod to the owning NuclioFunction and cron trigger. 2) Contain: suspend/delete the offending CronJob (kubectl delete cronjob), delete the NuclioFunction, and rotate the pod serviceaccount token / bound token if it was read. 3) Hunt: enumerate all CronJobs in the nuclio namespace lacking ownerReferences, review other functions' cron trigger event.headers/event.body for metacharacters, and pivot on outbound connections from the same pod (UC5).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "--header"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("$(", ")", "`", ";", "&&")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--header"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("$(", ")", "`", ";", "&&")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Egress from Nuclio CronJob curl process reading serviceaccount token to public IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a curl process that read the serviceaccount token (the injected command) with an outbound connection to a non-private IP within a short window — the token/secret exfiltration step of CVE-2026-52831 RCE. Multi-stage correlation on the same host/pod. Rationale: Ties the injected token-reading curl (from UC1) to a public egress within 5 minutes — the exfiltration shape of the RCE. Uses the exact token path and curl process; RFC1918 exclusion isolates external destinations. CIM Network_Traffic field names may need site-local mapping. Empty CloudWatch/Sigma (multi-stage, non-AWS).
ATT&CKT1020 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Function legitimately curls an external webhook/API as its designed behaviour
  • Cron trigger intentionally targeting a public endpoint
  • Egress through a NAT/CDN/proxy destination that looks public
  • Outbound telemetry from a sidecar that also happens to read the token
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl endswith ".svc.cluster.local" or RemoteIP startswith "100.64.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the same host/pod both read the serviceaccount token and made the external connection; resolve the destination IP/URL and check reputation. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress, kill the CronJob/pod, and rotate the serviceaccount token and any secrets the pod could reach. 3) Hunt: pull all destinations contacted by curl processes on nuclio pods, look for repeated beaconing to the same external IP, and cross-reference UC4 for downstream API abuse with the stolen token.
let TokenReads = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("$(", ")", "`", ";", "&&")
    | project TokenReadTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName == "curl"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| join kind=inner TokenReads on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (TokenReadTime .. TokenReadTime + 5m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let TokenReads = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("$(", ")", "`", ";", "&&")
    | project TokenReadTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr !startswith "10." and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.16." and DstIpAddr !startswith "127."

| where TimeGenerated between (TokenReadTime .. TokenReadTime + 5m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI Coding Agents Found Triggering Endpoint Security Rules Built to Catch Attackers

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Sophos looked at a week of its own endpoint data and found that AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenAI Codex are setting off detection rules written to catch human intruders. The agents are not malicious. They just do a lot of things that, to a behavioral engine, look exactly like an attack. Decrypting browser credentials, listing what sits in Windows' credential store,

DPAPI browser-credential decrypt via PowerShell (GStack /browse skill under AI coding agent) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact PowerShell one-liner GStack's /browse skill runs under Claude Code/Cursor to unlock Chromium credential data: Add-Type System.Security then ProtectedData::Unprotect on a base64 blob. Detects browser-credential decryption regardless of whether an AI agent or an attacker drove it, while surfacing the agent parent for triage. Rationale: Uses the verbatim GStack /browse command signature from the Sophos blog (ProtectedData::Unprotect + FromBase64String under powershell), which is the highest-fidelity string in the article; the AgentLineage tag distinguishes benign agent automation from real theft without dropping either. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer's Claude Code running GStack /browse for legitimate browser automation
  • Password managers or browser-profile migration utilities that legitimately DPAPI-decrypt saved logins
  • Authorized red-team/pentest tooling exercising browser credential extraction
  • Security research or QA reproducing the Sophos finding
  • Backup/sync tooling re-protecting DPAPI blobs on the same user context
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcessParentFileName — if the parent is claude.exe/cursor.exe/codex it is likely benign agent automation; confirm the logged-on user actually runs a coding agent. 2) Contain: if the parent is NOT a known agent (real theft), isolate the host and force-reset the browser-stored credentials and any SSO sessions decrypted. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for cmdkey /list, certutil/bitsadmin downloads, and startup-folder writes within the same session to separate agent noise from an intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "Unprotect"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "FromBase64String"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe","node.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has "System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData" and CommandLine has "Unprotect" and CommandLine has "FromBase64String"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| extend AgentLineage = iff(ParentProcessName has_any ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, AgentLineage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Windows Credential Manager enumeration via cmdkey /list under coding agent AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts cmdkey.exe /list — Claude Code was observed enumerating everything Windows Credential Manager holds. Rare in normal user space; the AI-agent parent lineage is surfaced to separate benign agent recon from an attacker's credential survey. Rationale: cmdkey.exe /list is the literal command Sophos attributed to Claude Code enumerating Credential Manager; it is uncommon enough in user space to hunt broadly while tagging agent lineage for fast triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1555.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin auditing saved RDP / network credentials with cmdkey /list
  • Logon or provisioning scripts that inventory stored credentials
  • MDM/endpoint-management agents enumerating credential entries
  • A developer's coding agent legitimately checking cached credentials before an automation task
  • IT troubleshooting of Credential Manager / SSO issues
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain — a claude.exe/cursor.exe ancestor plus a developer user strongly implies benign agent recon; an interactive shell under a service or unexpected user warrants escalation. 2) Contain: if paired with credential decryption or exfil, isolate the host and rotate any credentials visible in Credential Manager for that user. 3) Hunt: search the same host/session for DPAPI browser decrypt (UC1), LOLBin downloads, and outbound connections to determine if enumeration led to use.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "cmdkey.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/list"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmdkey.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/list"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| extend AgentLineage = iff(ParentProcessName has_any ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, AgentLineage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
