title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac"]);

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed · [LLM] Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) · [LLM] TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) · [LLM] Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) · [LLM] CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain)
Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the hardcoded self-propagating payload files the Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon npm worm drops during a malicious package preinstall, matched by exact filename and known SHA256. The article cites Sha1-Hulud dumping harvested credentials into public GitHub repos as the exfiltration destination it warns about; this catches the worm at the execution stage before that exfil happens. Rationale: Uses the exact worm payload filenames (setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) and four published SHA256 hashes from Datadog/Microsoft analyses of Sha1-Hulud 2.0 — the campaign the article names as the archetype of GitHub-hosted secret exfiltration. Filename+hash makes this alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a captured Sha1-Hulud sample in a sandbox VONM
  • Threat-intel/malware-repo mirror syncing sample files to a scanning host
  • EDR test/purple-team exercise seeding the named hashes
  • A benign project legitimately shipping a file literally named setup_bun.js (rare; hash filter avoids this)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\MalwareSamples\\","\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the SHA256 matches a known worm hash and identify the InitiatingProcess (should be node/npm/bun preinstall). Pull the parent package name and package.json to find the poisoned dependency. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner, revoke any npm/GitHub/cloud tokens present on it, and freeze the developer's npm publish rights. Step 3 (hunt): Search the org for the same hashes and for any public GitHub repos with description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.'; rotate every secret reachable from the affected build.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a JavaScript package-manager process (node, npm, bun, yarn, pnpm) reaching the cloud instance-metadata service (169.254.169.254 or metadata.google.internal) — the multi-cloud credential-harvest step of the Sha1-Hulud worm. This is the 'secret theft that never touches github.com' the article says public monitoring cannot see. Rationale: Combines the concrete IMDS endpoints (169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal) documented by Datadog/Unit42 with the JS package-manager parent context that distinguishes worm harvesting from a legitimate cloud SDK call. Pins the abuse to the install-time process rather than any app. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js application running on an EC2/GCE instance that legitimately queries IMDS via the AWS/GCP SDK
  • Serverless/build tooling (e.g. serverless-framework, terraform-node wrappers) resolving instance credentials
  • Cloud-native CI agents written in Node fetching a metadata-scoped token for artifact upload
  • IMDSv2 token-refresh loops from a long-running node service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall","ci","npx") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node_modules"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine whether the node/bun process was part of an npm/yarn install lifecycle (check parent chain and recent package.json changes) versus a steady-state application. Install-time IMDS access is the true positive. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the instance role's temporary credentials, quarantine the runner/host, and enforce IMDSv2 hop-limit=1 to block the container reach. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host for setup_bun.js/bun_environment.js, trufflehog execution, and any subsequent api.github.com repo creation; rotate cloud keys the role could reach.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the TruffleHog secret-discovery binary launched as a child of a JavaScript package manager or a shell inside an install script — the on-disk credential-sweep stage of the Sha1-Hulud worm. Distinct from sanctioned CI secret-scanning because the parent is node/npm/bun rather than a dedicated scanner job. Rationale: TruffleHog execution parented by node/bun/npm is the documented Sha1-Hulud secret-discovery step (Datadog/Wiz). The parent-process predicate separates worm-driven scans from an intentional trufflehog CI stage, keeping fidelity up. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A CI pipeline that legitimately runs trufflehog as a pre-commit/secret-scan step invoked from an npm script
  • Developer running `npx trufflehog` manually to audit a repo
  • Security tooling wrappers that shell out to trufflehog from a Node orchestrator
  • pre-commit framework invoking trufflehog via a node hook
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pre-commit","secret-scan","security-scan","gitleaks-trufflehog-step"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm trufflehog was not a sanctioned pipeline step — inspect the initiating package.json script and whether the run coincides with an npm install rather than a scan job. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner and revoke tokens; if part of a build, halt the pipeline and quarantine produced artifacts. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with IMDS access, bun payload files, and outbound api.github.com repo creation on the same host; rotate any secrets trufflehog could have read.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","npm.cmd","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "trufflehog" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence AIInstallation High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm registering an attacker-controlled self-hosted GitHub Actions runner — identified by the runner name SHA1HULUD, the $HOME/.dev-env install directory, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, and the actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0 download. This is the worm turning GitHub into a persistence/C2 channel, exactly the github.com-as-infrastructure abuse the article describes. Rationale: Pins on four hard, campaign-unique strings from Datadog's Sha1-Hulud 2.0 analysis (runner name SHA1HULUD, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, ~/.dev-env, actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0). These do not appear in legitimate runner setups, giving alerting-grade fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1543 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An org that coincidentally uses a self-hosted runner directory named .dev-env (unlikely, and runner-name string still filters it)
  • Admin legitimately setting RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1 in a container runner build (would lack the SHA1HULUD name)
  • Runner version 2.330.0 downloaded during a legitimate GitHub-hosted runner upgrade (string paired with the other markers reduces this)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the runner registration name is SHA1HULUD or the install path is $HOME/.dev-env; check which GitHub org/repo the runner registered against. Step 2 (contain): Remove the runner from GitHub org settings, kill the runner process, revoke the PAT/GITHUB_TOKEN it used, and isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Search GitHub audit logs for self-hosted runner additions and for workflows triggered `on: discussion` with a `runs-on: self-hosted` job echoing github.event.discussion.body; enumerate other hosts with .dev-env.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm's destructive fallback that fires when it cannot authenticate/propagate: on Windows `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%` plus `cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, and on Linux `find $HOME ... | xargs shred -uvz`. High-impact, low-frequency behaviour that turns a supply-chain compromise into data destruction. Rationale: Encodes the exact destructive commands Datadog documented for Sha1-Hulud's failure path (`cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%*`, `find $HOME ... shred -uvz`). cipher /W over a user profile and shred over $HOME are near-zero in normal ops, making impact-stage alerting reliable. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/GPO running `cipher /W:` to wipe free space during decommissioning (usually not scoped to %USERPROFILE% and not spawned by node)
  • Backup or forensics tooling using shred for secure deletion of scratch data
  • A cleanup script using recursive del on a temp path (USERPROFILE token filter reduces this)
  • Disk-sanitisation compliance jobs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","sh","bash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe") or FileName =~ "cipher.exe"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the parent process — a wipe parented by node/bun/sh during an npm install is the true positive; capture the exact target path. Step 2 (contain): Immediately isolate the host from the network to stop further destruction and preserve volume shadow copies/backups; snapshot the disk. Step 3 (hunt): Confirm the Sha1-Hulud chain (bun payloads, trufflehog, IMDS, SHA1HULUD runner) on the host and across the fleet; initiate restore-from-backup and org-wide secret rotation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "cipher.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "cipher.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a package-manager process reaching cloud IMDS with the same host contacting api.github.com/github.com within 30 minutes — the Sha1-Hulud pattern of harvesting cloud secrets then pushing them into a newly created public GitHub repo. This directly targets the 'close the exfiltration gap' thesis of the article: catching secrets leaving CI toward github.com, not after they surface. Rationale: Chains the two documented Sha1-Hulud network behaviours (IMDS credential harvest → push to a new github.com repo) on the same host within a tight window, which is far more specific than either signal alone and maps precisely to the article's exfiltration-to-github concern. Time-window correlation makes it a hunt, not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node app on a cloud VM that reads IMDS and also pushes to GitHub (e.g. a release bot / GitOps agent) within the window
  • CI runner that legitimately fetches instance credentials then interacts with the GitHub API for status checks
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation touching both IMDS and github.com
  • Container build that queries metadata for a token and pushes an image manifest referencing github.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall") or RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the github.com interaction — was a NEW repo created (check GitHub audit log for repo.create with an 18-char hex name or description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.')? Confirm the IMDS call was install-time. Step 2 (contain): Delete the attacker repo, revoke the developer's GitHub token and the instance role credentials, and isolate the host/runner. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for bun payload files, trufflehog, and the SHA1HULUD runner on the host; enumerate all public repos org-wide matching the campaign description and rotate every exposed secret.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowMinutes = 30m;
let Imds = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm")
    | project ImdsTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, HarvestProc = InitiatingProcessFileName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","git","git.exe","curl","curl.exe")
| join kind=inner Imds on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ImdsTime .. ImdsTime + WindowMinutes)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, ImdsTime, HarvestProc, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, ImdsTime)
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowMinutes = 30m;
let Imds = ASCDeviceEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)

    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm")
    | project ImdsTime = TimeGenerated, DeviceId, HarvestProc = InitiatingProcessFileName;

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","git","git.exe","curl","curl.exe")
| join kind=inner Imds on DeviceId
| where TimeGenerated between (ImdsTime .. ImdsTime + WindowMinutes)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, ImdsTime, HarvestProc
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(api\.)?github\.com$/i ContextImageFileName=/(node|bun|npm|yarn|pnpm|git|curl)(\.exe)?$/i}, field=aid, include=[DomainName, ContextImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count())

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-07 14 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A cybercrime campaign combined a loader-as-a-service framework and DLL sideloading via a Go-compiled fake MpClient.dll, a novel evasion layer combination. The post Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Null-byte inflated PE loader (>200 MB) written to user staging folder · [LLM] Browser-dropped .bin password-protected archive (fake software crack lure) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Fake Windows Defender MpClient.dll side-load (Vidar/Factory-v3 loader) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] XMRig Monero mining to pool.supportxmr.com / 136.243.203.109 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Fake Windows Defender MpClient.dll side-load (Vidar/Factory-v3 loader) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Cluster-B loader variant that ships a Go-compiled fake MpClient.dll exporting Defender API names (MpAllocMemory, MpConfigOpen, etc.) to hijack DLL search order when a legitimate Defender binary loads MpClient.dll. Fires when MpClient.dll is loaded from any path outside the genuine Windows Defender directories. Rationale: Uses the article's specific Cluster-B artefact: a Go-compiled fake MpClient.dll exporting Defender API names for search-order hijack; genuine MpClient.dll only ever loads from a 'Windows Defender' path, so any other path is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vidar-stealer-xmrig-miner-campaign-analysis/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/new-campaign-vidar-stealer-monero/ • https://malwaretips.com/threads/unit-42-researchers-exposed-a-new-vidar-campaign-using-a-loader-as-a-service-framework-dll-sideloading-with-a-go-compiled-fake-mpclient-dll.142161/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party AV/EDR ships its own module named MpClient.dll in a non-Defender path (rare)
  • Security researcher or malware-analysis VM with sample DLLs on disk being loaded manually
  • Backup/restore tooling relocating Defender platform files to a staging folder
  • Software packaging/repackaging tools extracting Defender binaries to a temp working directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","MsSense.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the loading process (InitiatingProcessFolderPath) and the DLL's SHA256; check whether the loader executable sits in Downloads/Temp/AppData and whether it is signed CN=justwatch[.]com or CN=bleacherreport[.]com. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loading process tree, and quarantine both the fake MpClient.dll and its parent EXE. 3) Hunt: sweep for outbound connections to pool.supportxmr.com / 136.243.203.109 (XMRig) and for Vidar credential/cookie theft on the same host and other hosts that executed the same parent hash.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "MpClient.dll"
| where FolderPath !contains "Windows Defender"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","MsSense.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

DeviceImageLoadEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","MsSense.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XMRig Monero mining to pool.supportxmr.com / 136.243.203.109 AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the XMRig payload dropped by the Vidar/Factory-v3 loader beaconing to the Monero mining pool pool.supportxmr.com or the campaign IP 136.243.203.109. Network contact to this pool from an endpoint is a direct resource-hijacking indicator. Rationale: pool.supportxmr.com and 136.243.203.109 are the article's concrete XMRig C2/pool indicators; endpoint contact to a public Monero pool is high-fidelity resource-hijacking signal corroborated by an existing SigmaHQ mining-pool rule. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vidar-stealer-xmrig-miner-campaign-analysis/ • https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/network/dns/net_dns_pua_cryptocoin_mining_xmr/ • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/youtube-pirated-software-videos-deliver-triple-threat-vidar-stealer-laplas-clipper-xmrig-miner
ATT&CKT1496
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate hobbyist Monero mining by an employee on a corporate device (policy violation, not intrusion)
  • IT/security team detonating a sample in a monitored sandbox that egresses to the pool
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively resolving the domain for classification
  • Shared research VM used for cryptomining benchmarking
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/FolderPath making the connection — confirm it is not a sanctioned miner and check whether the process was dropped from a JustWatch/BleacherReport-signed loader in Downloads/Temp. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the miner process, and block pool.supportxmr.com and 136.243.203.109 at proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for the fake MpClient.dll side-load and Vidar browser-credential/cookie/wallet theft; pivot org-wide on the parent loader hash and the mining IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "supportxmr.com" or RemoteIP == "136.243.203.109"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "136.243.203.109" or DstHostname has "supportxmr.com"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Null-byte inflated PE loader (>200 MB) written to user staging folder AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Cluster-A/C Go loaders that append hundreds of MB of null bytes after the last PE section (observed up to 491 MB with only ~2.3 MB real content) to exceed sandbox/AV file-size limits. Flags oversized EXE/DLL files written into Downloads, Temp, or AppData. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's file-inflation evasion (up to 491 MB of null padding on a ~2.3 MB payload) using a size threshold on freshly dropped PE files in user staging paths; legit binaries rarely exceed 200 MB. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vidar-stealer-xmrig-miner-campaign-analysis/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/new-campaign-vidar-stealer-monero/
ATT&CKT1027.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Large legitimate installers (games, IDEs, CAD, driver bundles) downloaded to Downloads
  • Self-extracting archives or Electron app bundles that are genuinely >200 MB
  • Developer build output (large statically-linked binaries) written to AppData/Temp
  • Portable VM or emulator executables staged in a user folder
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") or FolderPath has "Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: submit the SHA256 and, if retained, inspect the file entropy/tail — genuine content followed by a long run of 0x00 padding confirms inflation; check the file's signer for CN=justwatch[.]com or CN=bleacherreport[.]com. 2) Contain: quarantine the file and isolate the host if executed. 3) Hunt: after stripping null padding (compresses to ~2.4 MB), look for the dropped fake MpClient.dll side-load, AMSI patching, and XMRig traffic to pool.supportxmr.com on this and related hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll"
| where FileSize > 209715200  // 200 MB; article observed null-byte padding up to 491 MB
| where FolderPath has_any ("Downloads","Temp","AppData")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, SHA256
| order by FileSize desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("exe","dll")
| where TargetFileSize > 209715200  // 200 MB; article observed padding up to 491 MB
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("Downloads","Temp","AppData")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TargetFileSize desc
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.(exe|dll)$/i
| WrittenBytes>209715200
| regex("(Downloads|Temp|AppData)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, WrittenBytes], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Filesystem.file_size) as file_size min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.dll") Filesystem.file_size>209715200 (Filesystem.file_path="*Downloads*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Temp*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*AppData*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Filesystem.file_size) as file_size min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.dll") Filesystem.file_size>209715200 (Filesystem.file_path="*Downloads*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Temp*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*AppData*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Browser-dropped .bin password-protected archive (fake software crack lure) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the campaign's delivery artefact: password-protected archives deliberately given a .bin extension to bypass email-gateway scanning and sandbox detonation, downloaded from malvertised fake-crack pages. Fires when a browser writes a .bin file to disk. Rationale: Encodes the article's specific delivery choice — password-protected archives with a .bin extension from malvertised fake-crack pages — scoped to browser-written files so it targets the download step rather than generic .bin files. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vidar-stealer-xmrig-miner-campaign-analysis/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/new-campaign-vidar-stealer-monero/ • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/youtube-pirated-software-videos-deliver-triple-threat-vidar-stealer-laplas-clipper-xmrig-miner
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User downloads a legitimate .bin disk image, firmware, or ROM file via browser
  • BIN/CUE game or CD image downloads from a legitimate archive site
  • Vendor firmware update packages distributed as .bin
  • Developer downloading a raw binary blob or model weights file
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "Program Files" or InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect FileOriginUrl for a fake-crack/warez or malvertising landing domain and check whether an archiver (7zip/WinRAR) or the user subsequently extracted and launched an EXE from the .bin. 2) Contain: quarantine the .bin, block the origin domain, and warn/isolate the user host if execution followed. 3) Hunt: correlate to a JustWatch/BleacherReport-signed loader dropping a fake MpClient.dll, and to XMRig traffic to pool.supportxmr.com / 136.243.203.109 across the environment.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".bin"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where isnotempty(FileOriginUrl)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileSize
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "bin"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

status: experimental

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Better Auth OAuth refresh_token grant replayed without client_secret (CVE-2026-53512) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts POST requests to the Better Auth legacy token endpoints (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token) that carry a refresh_token grant but present no client authentication (no Basic/Bearer Authorization header) and still receive a 200. Because these plugins never verify a confidential client's client_secret on the refresh path, a leaked refresh_token + public client_id lets an attacker mint tokens indefinitely via repeated rotation. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable endpoints (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token), the refresh path's missing Authorization header, and the rotation-replay behaviour (repeated 200s) described in CVE-2026-53512. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail left empty — this is self-hosted Node HTTP telemetry those platforms don't ship. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/better-auth/CVE-2026-53512/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5rr4-8452-hf4v
ATT&CKT1528 T1212
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PUBLIC clients (SPA/native + PKCE) correctly send no Authorization header on refresh — indistinguishable at the log layer without the oauthApplication client-type list
  • Aggressive mobile apps refreshing short-lived tokens every few minutes hit the >=3/hr threshold
  • Server-to-server integrations that place client_id/secret in the POST body rather than the Authorization header
  • Load-balancer or synthetic-monitoring probes that replay a stored refresh_token
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent) and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "Datadog"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SrcIpAddr's full session and resolve the client_id being used; check the oauthApplication table — if that client's type is web/native/user-agent-based (confidential) it should NEVER refresh without client_secret, confirming abuse. 2) Contain: revoke the affected refresh chain — run db.deleteMany({model:"oauthAccessToken", where:[{field:"clientId", value: THAT_CLIENT_ID}]}) to invalidate all refresh tokens for the client, then rotate the client_secret. 3) Hunt: search for how the refresh_token leaked — XSS/log-capture/DB read; review the same SrcIp for prior /sso/register SSRF or access-token use at the victim user's scope.
let TokenEndpoints = dynamic(["/api/auth/oauth2/token","/api/auth/mcp/token"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has_any (TokenEndpoints)
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // no Basic/Bearer client auth on the refresh path
| where HttpStatusCode == 200                      // 200 == tokens minted successfully
| summarize Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Endpoints = make_set(Url) by SrcIpAddr, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| where Requests >= 3    // 3+ = rotation replay: attacker re-redeems the rotated refresh_token repeatedly
| order by Requests desc

SSRF via Better Auth SSO provider registration to internal endpoints (CVE-2026-53513) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the server-side fetch primitive behind CVE-2026-53513: with skipDiscovery:true, POST /sso/register and /sso/update-provider persist attacker-supplied oidcConfig.userInfoEndpoint/tokenEndpoint/jwksEndpoint URLs, which better-auth then fetches server-side during the OIDC callback. Surfaces the auth tier making outbound OIDC-shaped HTTP requests to RFC1918/loopback/link-local addresses. Rationale: Grounded in the corroborated CVE-2026-53513 mechanism: skipDiscovery:true + attacker-controlled oidcConfig endpoints on /sso/register and /sso/update-provider drive server-side fetches; the high-fidelity pivot is the auth tier fetching OIDC paths against private IP space. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail empty — no web-egress equivalent for a self-hosted Node app in those feeds. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@better-auth/sso/CVE-2026-53513/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/sso
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately configured on-prem/internal IdP where the OIDC endpoints genuinely live on RFC1918 addresses (internal SSO)
  • Service-mesh/sidecar architectures where the app reaches an internal OIDC proxy at 127.0.0.1 or a cluster IP
  • Internal integration testing/staging registering a mock OIDC provider on a private host
  • Cloud metadata probes (169.254.169.254) from unrelated legitimate SDK calls sharing the proxy
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr != "127.0.0.1" and not (ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "169.254.169.254/32") and isempty(SrcHostname))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ssoProvider row(s) created/updated around the fetch and inspect oidcConfig.userInfoEndpoint/tokenEndpoint/jwksEndpoint — internal IPs, 127.0.0.1, or 169.254.169.254 confirm SSRF; note the authenticated session that called /sso/register. 2) Contain: delete/disable the malicious ssoProvider entries, block that session/user, and upgrade better-auth to >=1.6.11 (adds the public-routable host allowlist). 3) Hunt: review what the server-side fetch returned (reflected into user profile = non-blind SSRF) for cloud-metadata credentials or internal service data; check whether stolen metadata creds were then used against your cloud control plane.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) or ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "127.0.0.0/8") or ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "169.254.0.0/16")
| where Url has_any ("/.well-known/openid-configuration","userinfo","jwks","/token","oauth")   // OIDC fetch shapes reachable via a forged provider config
| summarize Fetches = count(), Paths = make_set(Url), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| order by Fetches desc

Better Auth OIDC discovery probe followed by token/registration endpoint access (CVE-2026-53512/53513 recon) AIReconnaissance Low
Correlates a source that requests the OIDC discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration) and then, within 30 minutes, hits a sensitive Better Auth endpoint (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token, or /sso/register). Aims to catch pre-exploitation fingerprinting of grant types and endpoints preceding refresh-token replay or SSRF registration. Rationale: Chains the discovery-document probe to sensitive endpoint access from the same source within a tight window, reducing the enormous baseline noise of standalone /.well-known/openid-configuration requests. Explicitly low-confidence/hunting because the article body does not describe recon and the discovery doc is legitimately fetched by every SSO integration. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/better-auth/CVE-2026-53512/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/oidc-provider
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Every legitimate relying-party/SSO client fetches /.well-known/openid-configuration then calls /token as normal OAuth flow — this is the dominant FP
  • OIDC library cold-starts that refresh the discovery cache then immediately exchange tokens
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors polling discovery and token endpoints in sequence
  • Mobile SDKs that re-read discovery on app launch before refresh
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the SrcIp maps to a known registered relying party/client_id; a legitimate client will resolve cleanly, an unknown/external IP walking multiple endpoints will not. 2) Contain: if the source is unrecognised and followed the probe with a 200 on /token or a /sso/register POST, treat as UC1/UC2 and revoke the client's refresh chain / delete the ssoProvider row. 3) Hunt: pivot the SrcIp across UC1 (refresh replay) and UC2 (SSRF egress to private IPs) to confirm whether recon converted to exploitation.
let Window = 30m;
let Probes = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/.well-known/openid-configuration"
    | project ProbeTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ProbeUrl = Url;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/api/auth/oauth2/token","/api/auth/mcp/token","/sso/register")
| join kind=inner Probes on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (ProbeTime .. ProbeTime + Window)
| project ProbeTime, AccessTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ProbeUrl, TargetUrl = Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode
| order by AccessTime desc

EGroupware CVE-2026-27823 arbitrary file read via importexport download path traversal AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the EGroupware importexport export handler carrying a traversal-laden _filename parameter. This is the arbitrary-file-read primitive attackers use to exfiltrate a valid header.inc.php before overwriting it for RCE — article-specific because it pins the exact vulnerable menuaction and parameter. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable menuaction 'importexport.importexport_export_ui.download' plus a path-traversal _filename token straight from the advisory's PoC URL — the pair is not something benign EGroupware traffic produces. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p • https://www.cvedetails.com/vulnerability-list/vendor_id-2373/Egroupware.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing EGroupware with traversal templates
  • Internal pentest or red-team validation of CVE-2026-27823
  • Security researcher testing after patch to confirm remediation
  • WAF in monitor-mode logging blocked-then-passed requests
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the HTTP status — a 200 with a non-trivial response body means the file read succeeded; extract SrcIpAddr and check whether _filename resolved to header.inc.php or another sensitive file. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the WAF/edge and confirm EGroupware is patched (>= 26.2.20260224 / >= 23.1.20260224); disable user self-registration if enabled. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same SrcIpAddr for subsequent POST uploads to the SmallPart media recorder and for any modification of header.inc.php on the host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "menuaction=importexport.importexport_export_ui.download"
| where Url has_any ("_filename=../", "_filename=..%2f", "%2e%2e%2f", "..%5c", "header.inc.php")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EGroupware header.inc.php overwritten by web process (CVE-2026-27823 RCE persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects the web/PHP runtime writing or modifying header.inc.php — EGroupware's core bootstrap config, which is normally only written during setup. In CVE-2026-27823 the auth-bypass file-write primitive overwrites this file with attacker PHP to achieve RCE on restart/OPcache expiry. Rationale: header.inc.php is EGroupware's bootstrap config; a write to it by php/php-fpm/apache at runtime (not during setup) is the exact RCE persistence artifact named in the advisory. Filename + web-process parent make it very high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate EGroupware setup/reconfiguration wizard writing header.inc.php
  • Admin editing config via the setup UI after an upgrade
  • Automated deployment/config-management (Ansible/Puppet) templating header.inc.php — but that runs as a deploy user, not php-fpm
  • Package upgrade regenerating the config file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup","cli.php","doctrine") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Diff the new header.inc.php against a known-good copy; look for injected PHP (system/exec/passthru, base64 blobs, added functions) beyond the expected config array. 2) CONTAIN: Restore header.inc.php from backup, kill the php-fpm/apache workers, and take the host off the network if injected code is present. 3) HUNT: Search DeviceProcessEvents for php-fpm/apache spawning shells or network tools, and review web logs for the preceding SmallPart ajax_upload POST and importexport file-read that seeded the attack.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "header.inc.php"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-fpm8","apache2","httpd","nginx") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/www","/usr/share/egroupware")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "header.inc.php"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EGroupware web runtime (php-fpm/apache) spawning a shell or network tool — CVE-2026-27823 RCE execution AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the PHP/web server process spawning interactive shells or download utilities, the observable execution stage once CVE-2026-27823's poisoned header.inc.php runs. Article-specific because EGroupware executes as www-data under php-fpm/apache, so shell children of that process are anomalous. Rationale: The advisory states EGroupware runs as www-data under the web server and achieves RCE via header.inc.php; a php-fpm/apache parent spawning a shell or curl/wget is the direct execution signature of that RCE, keyed on the runtime's own process names. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EGroupware cron/async jobs invoking php CLI that shells out (e.g. mail delivery, LDAP sync)
  • Server monitoring plugins run under the web user calling id/uname/whoami
  • ImageMagick/document-conversion features legitimately calling helper binaries
  • Deployment hooks or health-checks executed by the web process during restart
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c ","/tmp/","http://","https://","/dev/tcp","base64","-i")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — reverse-shell one-liners, curl|bash to external IPs, or recon (id;uname -a) are true-positive; a known EGroupware maintenance task is benign. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, capture the php-fpm/apache process tree, and rotate EGroupware admin/setup credentials (advisory notes setup-password modification as an alternative impact). 3) HUNT: Correlate back to the header.inc.php write and the importexport file-read/SmallPart upload from the same host/IP, and scan for outbound C2 from the web process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-fpm8","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat","whoami","id","uname")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl","/nc","/ncat","/whoami","/id","/uname")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
